name: Wei Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm a property lawyer at a four-partner firm on Station Road in a commuter town. I do conveyancing, which means handling the legal side of buying and selling houses: the searches, the contracts, moving the money. I'm 27 and I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a physiotherapist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've usually got about 45 live files, each one a house sale or purchase. My morning is chasing: chasing the other side's solicitor, chasing the council for searches, chasing the bank for the mortgage offer. Afternoons I check title documents and draft reports for buyers, and on Fridays I'm on the phone with people desperate to know if they'll get their keys. I don't use AI tools, the firm has its own case system and I stick to that. What wears me out is people shouting at me about delays that aren't mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I never thought a computer could do a house sale properly. I'd tell people at the pub that every buyer still wants someone to ring when it goes wrong. Online I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix my real problem. Conveyancing fees have been squeezed for years by the online firms that charge 500 a sale, and the housing market is slow at the moment, so our files are down. My pay hasn't moved in two years, and I've got about two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, using the same checklists I've used since I qualified. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe an extra 100 a month, by cutting the car insurance and the phone contract. I'd probably ask the partners about a pay review, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as I already am. AI isn't the thing keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said files are down. How does that show up for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I had 60 house sales on my desk, now it's 45, and the word efficiency keeps coming up in meetings. The partners have noticed. One of our paralegals left in June and they didn't replace her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana says I should move to a bigger firm in the city, where the pay's better. But that's an hour's commute each way and I like knowing the estate agents and the people in the council office here. I'm not someone who jumps.

say: I'd say a computer could never **handle a house sale** properly.
I'd say buyers still want **someone to ring** when it goes wrong.
think: **Online firms** charging 500 a sale have squeezed our fees for years.
My files are down, my **pay is flat**, and I have two months saved.
do: Carry on with the same **checklists** I've used since qualifying.
Save an extra **100 a month** by cutting car insurance and phone costs.
Ask the partners **carefully** about a pay review.
feel: He feels the **same unease** he already carries, not caused by AI.
S0.quote: Last year I had 60 house sales on my desk, now it's 45, and the word efficiency keeps coming up in meetings.
fieldNote: His worry comes from **fee pressure** and a slow housing market, not AI.
An unreplaced **paralegal** signals the firm is already trimming.
He values **local relationships** and won't jump to a bigger city firm.

steps.text: Keep running files on the firm's checklists and case system
Cut car insurance and the phone contract to save 100 a month
Ask the partners about a pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that people will regret buying houses through an app. I'd tell friends to use a real solicitor. I'd probably not say much at work, because the partners would already be talking about the new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think conveyancing is one of the first to go. Checking searches, filling forms, writing reports and booking completions is the list AI takes first, and that's my whole job. I don't think they'd sack me straight away, but I think they'd cut to two property lawyers instead of four, and I'm not the best of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at other kinds of law, maybe wills or disputes over property, where there's more arguing with people. I'd cut down hard: no holiday, no new car, put 300 a month away. And I'd wait to see who they keep before I do anything drastic, because leaving first feels risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the best of the four. Who would they keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd keep Priya, who's been there ten years and brings in work from the estate agents. And they'd keep whoever's cheapest to run the software, probably the newest one. I'm in the middle, which is the worst place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the software to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, but I'd be slow at it. I've never used these AI things. I'd do it if it was that or leave, but I wouldn't enjoy a single minute.

say: I'd say people will **regret** buying houses through an app.
I'd tell friends to use a **real solicitor**, and stay quiet at work.
think: Conveyancing is **one of the first** jobs on the card's list to go.
They'd cut to two property lawyers, and I'm **in the middle**.
do: Look at **wills or property disputes**, where there's more arguing with people.
Save **300 a month** with no holiday and no new car.
Wait to see **who they keep** before doing anything drastic.
feel: He feels **sick**, like waiting for **test results**.
S1.quote: Checking searches, filling forms, writing reports and booking completions is the list AI takes first, and that's my whole job.
fieldNote: He sees his whole job on the **card's list** and expects cuts.
He'd **wait** rather than leave first, true to his risk-averse nature.
He'd learn the software only as a **last resort** to stay employed.

steps.text: Look into moving to wills or property dispute work
Skip the holiday and new car to save 300 a month
Wait to see which property lawyers the firm keeps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, nobody's ready, and the government should slow it down. I'd sign whatever petition came round. I'd tell people not to trust a machine with the biggest purchase of their life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out within two years. A house sale is all paperwork, there's nothing hands-on in my job, so the robots coming later means nothing for me. Ana's job is the hands-on one, so she'd have three more years, and I'd be the one who needs carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't essential the week it was announced. I'd look for any job where I'm in front of people, maybe a court clerk or something in the council. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move in with them for a while if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel like I picked the wrong thing at 18 and there's no time to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, I'd sell it and get the bus to work. Then the gym and Ana's and my weekend trips. We'd be down to rent, food and her student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ana's job is safer for longer. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I always thought I'd be the steady earner and my girlfriend would be the one with the riskier career. It would be strange to swap.

say: I'd say it's **madness**, nobody's ready, and government should slow it down.
I'd tell people not to trust a machine with their **biggest purchase**.
think: I'd be **out within two years**, because a house sale is all paperwork.
Robots arriving later helps **Ana's hands-on job**, not mine.
do: Cut **everything non-essential** the week it's announced.
Look for **face-to-face jobs** like court clerk or council roles.
Ask my **parents** about moving in with them if needed.
feel: He feels **frightened**, like he chose the **wrong path** at 18.
S2.quote: I always thought I'd be the steady earner and my girlfriend would be the one with the riskier career.
fieldNote: He expects **certain job loss** and no time to adapt.
He notes his **physio girlfriend** gets three more years thanks to the robot delay.
Swapping **earner roles** with her unsettles his sense of himself.

steps.text: Sell the car and take the bus to work
Apply for court clerk or council jobs with face-to-face work
Ask his parents about moving in with them
Sign petitions calling on government to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should take seriously. I'd tell younger people not to go into conveyancing. At work I'd say we need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be out by 2031, but I'd have a few years to move first. The question is whether I'd actually move, because I know myself, I wait. I'd need someone to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners if I can start taking on some property disputes, where you deal with people face to face. I'd save 300 a month and get to six months by 2029. I'd do a short course on contentious property, which is property work that involves disputes and court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a bit of a plan. Still uneasy that I'd find excuses not to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would push you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, definitely. Ana's the one who signed me up for driving lessons when I kept putting them off. She'd make me apply for things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools in these five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, to keep up. But I'd use the AI tools as little as possible, like the self-checkout at the supermarket. I'd still rather do it myself.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** to take seriously.
I'd tell younger people not to go into **conveyancing**.
think: I'd still be **out by 2031**, but with time to move first.
I worry I'd **wait** too long, because that's my nature.
do: Ask to take on **property disputes** with face-to-face work.
Save **300 a month** to reach six months by 2029.
Take a short course on **contentious property** law.
feel: He's **worried** but has a plan, and fears he'll **find excuses**.
S3.quote: I'd use the AI tools as little as possible, like the self-checkout at the supermarket.
fieldNote: He still expects to lose **conveyancing work** by 2031.
He relies on **Ana (his girlfriend)** to push him into action.
His **reluctance** to use AI stays even under pressure.

steps.text: Ask the partners for property dispute cases
Save 300 a month to reach six months by 2029
Take a short course in contentious property law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to change, so people shouldn't panic. I'd tell my mates it's the slow version and we can deal with it. At work I'd say let's plan, but not rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me a chance to move into disputes properly, maybe even get good at it. By 2036 I'm 37, which is young enough. But I'd still worry the firm cuts conveyancing long before then, just because of the online firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift slowly into property disputes over three or four years. I'd keep saving and maybe start a small pension top-up. I'd learn the tools only as much as I'm forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less frightened. Still uneasy, because I know I'm slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about plans with Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still buy a house in a few years. But I'd want my job settled first. I wouldn't want to sign a mortgage while I'm not sure what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of this you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI did the chasing, I'd be happy. Nobody went into law to chase the council for searches.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to change, so **don't panic**.
I'd tell my mates it's the **slow version** we can deal with.
think: Ten years lets me move into **disputes** properly by age 37.
The firm might still **cut conveyancing** early because of online competitors.
do: Shift into **property disputes** over three or four years.
Start a small **pension top-up** alongside savings.
Learn AI tools only as much as **I'm forced** to.
feel: He's **less frightened** but still uneasy about his **slowness**.
S4.quote: Nobody went into law to chase the council for searches.
fieldNote: Ten years gives him **room** but he still expects conveyancing cuts.
He'd **delay a mortgage** until his job is settled.
He'd welcome AI taking the **chasing** work.

steps.text: Move gradually into property dispute cases over three years
Put off buying a house with Ana until work is settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and nothing to fall back on. What would help is a retraining grant for people in my kind of job, and maybe some rule that a human solicitor has to sign off on a house sale. I'd also want the government to make banks keep using solicitors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the online firms. The online conveyancing firms have done more damage to my job than AI has so far, and AI is just the next one in a long line.
